item.title: oPt: West Bank and Gaza Strip: FAO Humanitarian response update, November 2026
item.description:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

• By mid-2026, conditional cash+ assistance from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) had enabled 1 700 farming households in the Gaza Strip to produce enough fresh vegetables to meet the annual vegetable intake requirements of an estimated 121 000 people, based on the dietary recommendations of FAO and the World Health Organization.1 Restoring full access to agricultural inputs could increase this figure to an estimated 284 000 people.

• Conditional cash+ assistance provided by FAO to livestock-keeping households in the Gaza Strip contributed to increases in the sheep (33 percent) and goat (8 percent) populations between November 2025 and May 2026, the first recorded increase since October 2023.2 However, the sheep and goat populations remain at approximately one-quarter and one-third of pre‑conflict levels, respectively.

• With improved security and access following the October 2025 ceasefire, FAO has distributed approximately 430 tonnes of animal feed per month, about four times the monthly volume distributed before the ceasefire.

• An FAO analysis found that every USD 1 invested in livestock protection in the Gaza Strip during 2024–2026 generated approximately USD 2.30 in livestock asset value.

item.title: DR Congo: Ituri: la MONUSCO renforce ses interventions pour protéger les civils face à la recrudescence des violences à Djugu
item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: UN Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

Face à la recrudescence des affrontements armés dans le territoire de Djugu, en Ituri, les Casques bleus bangladais de la MONUSCO ont mobilisé, le 22 novembre 2026, une base opérationnelle mobile afin de renforcer la protection des populations civiles dans les localités d’Akwe, de Damas et de Mbidjo, dans la région de Mongbwalu. Ce déploiement a notamment permis de faciliter, deux jours plus tard, l’évacuation de dix agents de santé engagés dans la riposte contre la maladie à virus Ebola.

Depuis plusieurs jours, la situation sécuritaire s’est fortement détériorée dans plusieurs localités du territoire de Djugu, notamment à Fataki, Bule et Gina, où des affrontements opposent les Forces armées de la République démocratique du Congo (FARDC) aux éléments du groupe armé Convention pour la révolution populaire (CRP). Le 18 novembre, de violents combats ont notamment été signalés aux environs de Bule et du site de déplacés de la plaine de Savo, qui accueille environ 70 000 personnes.

Ces violences ont provoqué de nouveaux déplacements de populations, y compris parmi des personnes ayant déjà fui l’insécurité. Vingt-quatre civils, dont treize femmes et trois enfants, ont notamment trouvé refuge auprès des Casques bleus de la MONUSCO à Bayoo.

En outre, les affrontements et les déplacements de populations signalés dans la zone d’Akwe, de Damas et de Mbidjo ont conduit le bataillon bangladais à déploiement rapide (BANRDB) de la MONUSCO à renforcer sa présence sur le terrain et à apporter une assistance aux personnes en difficulté, notamment aux personnels de santé.

L’intervention s’est toutefois heurtée à d’importantes contraintes logistiques. Le relief accidenté, le mauvais état des routes et la fragilité d’un pont en bois ont empêché les Casques bleus de poursuivre leur progression sur l’itinéraire initialement prévu. Ils ont alors exploré des solutions alternatives, tout en maintenant le contact avec les personnels de santé et l’équipe chargée de les accueillir, afin d’identifier un point de rencontre accessible.

Le 24 novembre, les Casques bleus ont ainsi pu rejoindre dix agents de santé, parmi lesquels un médecin et des infirmiers de l’hôpital général de référence d’Akwe. Ils les ont escortés jusqu’à l’hôpital de Mongbwalu, puis jusqu’à l’aire d’atterrissage des hélicoptères, en vue de leur évacuation par voie aérienne vers Bunia.

Engagés dans la riposte contre l’épidémie d’Ebola, ces agents de santé jouent un rôle essentiel auprès des populations déjà fragilisées par les violences et les déplacements. Cette intervention s’inscrit dans le cadre de l’appui de la MONUSCO aux efforts de riposte contre Ebola, notamment à travers la protection du personnel de santé et la sécurisation de l’accès aux soins pour les populations affectées par les violences.

Quatre jours plus tôt, le 20 novembre, les Casques bleus bangladais et népalais de la MONUSCO avaient facilité le retour sécurisé de 380 civils depuis Fataki jusqu’au site de déplacés de la plaine de Savo, après que des affrontements les avaient contraints à fuir. Les bénéficiaires et les autorités coutumières locales ont salué l’appui de la MONUSCO.

Dans ce contexte sécuritaire tendu, la MONUSCO a également renforcé ses patrouilles dans la zone afin de protéger les populations civiles contre les violences des groupes armés.

-Didier Vignon Dossou-Gbakon

item.title: DR Congo: Ituri: MONUSCO steps up interventions to protect civilians amid resurgence of violence in Djugu
item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: UN Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

In response to renewed armed clashes in Djugu Territory, Ituri Province, Bangladeshi peacekeepers serving with MONUSCO deployed a mobile operating base on 22 November 2026 to strengthen the protection of civilians in the localities of Akwe, Damas and Mbidjo, in the Mongbwalu area. The deployment notably helped facilitate the evacuation, two days later, of ten health workers involved in the response to the Ebola virus disease outbreak.

For several days, the security situation has deteriorated significantly in several localities across Djugu Territory, particularly in Fataki, Bule and Gina, where clashes have pitted the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) against elements of the armed group known as the Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP). On 18 November, heavy fighting was reported around Bule and the Savo Plain displacement site, which hosts approximately 70,000 people.

The violence has triggered further population displacement, including among people who had already fled insecurity. Twenty-four civilians, including thirteen women and three children, sought refuge with MONUSCO peacekeepers in Bayoo.

Furthermore, the clashes and population movements reported in the Akwe, Damas and Mbidjo areas prompted MONUSCO's Bangladeshi Rapid Deployment Battalion (BANRDB) to strengthen its presence on the ground and provide assistance to people in distress, particularly healthcare workers.

However, the operation faced significant logistical challenges. Difficult terrain, poor road conditions and the fragile state of a wooden bridge prevented the peacekeepers from continuing along their initially planned route. They therefore explored alternative options while maintaining contact with the healthcare workers and the team assigned to receive them, in order to identify an accessible meeting point.

On 24 November, the peacekeepers successfully reached ten healthcare workers, including a doctor and nurses from Akwe General Referral Hospital. They escorted them to Mongbwalu Hospital and then to the helicopter landing site, where they were scheduled to be evacuated by air to Bunia.

These healthcare workers, who are actively involved in the response to the Ebola outbreak, play a vital role in assisting communities already weakened by violence and displacement. This intervention is part of MONUSCO's support for Ebola response efforts, particularly through the protection of healthcare personnel and the facilitation of safe access to healthcare for populations affected by violence.

Four days earlier, on 20 November, Bangladeshi and Nepalese MONUSCO peacekeepers had facilitated the safe return of 380 civilians from Fataki to the Savo Plain displacement site after clashes had forced them to flee. The beneficiaries and local customary authorities expressed their appreciation for MONUSCO's support.

Against this backdrop of heightened insecurity, MONUSCO has also stepped up its patrols in the area to protect civilians from violence perpetrated by armed groups.

-Didier Vignon Dossou-Gbakon

item.title: Haiti: MSF teams treating alarming numbers of women for sexual violence in Port-au-Prince
item.description:
Country: Haiti
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

Port-au-Prince – On the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, the number of victims and survivors of sexual violence seeking care at Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) facilities in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, remains alarmingly high in 2026. Most of them have been forced to flee their homes, making them particularly vulnerable. In the absence of sufficient protection services, MSF is calling on state authorities, humanitarian organisations, and civil society to urgently increase the capacity for safe shelter, strengthen referrals to healthcare, and provide sustainable support to local organisations.

Despite repeated warnings from MSF and several organisations over several years about the scale of sexual violence and its consequences for people in Port-au-Prince, the need to care for victims and survivors continues to increase in 2026. The abuse and assault of mainly women and girls are taking place in a context of armed violence, population displacement, and major difficulties for people to access healthcare and protection, particularly shelter.

Between January and October 2026, 5,635 victims and survivors were treated in MSF facilities in the city, including 804 in July alone. These figures reflect the number of people who were able to access care, particularly at the Cité Soleil hospital and the Pran Men'm clinic. However, these figures do not represent the true scale of the violence, as not all victims are able to report it systematically.

One day, two armed men burst into my home... They beat me and they both sexually assaulted me.

A survivor of sexual violence MSF treated in Port-au-Prince

“Many victims and survivors are unable to reach our facilities in time and safely,” says Marie-Camille Gauthier Lessard, project coordinator at MSF’s Pran Men'm clinic. “More than 70 per cent of the victims and survivors cared for by MSF between January and July 2026 arrived after 120 hours, a critical time limit for certain emergency medical treatments.”

In the Haitian capital, armed violence is upending the living conditions of communities, forcing many families to flee their homes to seek refuge elsewhere.

“I was living in a working-class neighbourhood with my two children. One day, two armed men burst into my home; they forced the door and came in,” says a survivor MSF treated. “They beat me and they both sexually assaulted me. Then they ordered me to leave the neighbourhood, threatening to kill me and my children if I did not go.”

“The next day, I took refuge with a friend who lived in another working-class neighbourhood. One day, while she was away, armed men broke into her house and sexually assaulted me again,” the survivor continues. “Since then, life has lost all meaning. I wanted to end my life, but someone stopped me and reminded me that I have two children to raise.”

“Today, my daughter is growing up and I realise that we are still living in this area,” she continues. “I really do not feel safe.”

One of our patients told us that she had to lie on top of her own teenage daughters to allow them to sleep, as the only way to protect them from potential assaults.

Dr Claudia Lodesani, MSF medical coordinator in Port-au-Prince

Dr Claudia Lodesani, MSF medical coordinator in Port-au-Prince, describes the situation survivors find themselves in.

“Displaced people end up in makeshift shelters such as churches, schools or stadiums, which are most of the time unsanitary and unsuitable,” says Dr Lodesani. “In these places, women and girls are particularly vulnerable. One of our patients told us that she had to lie on top of her own teenage daughters to allow them to sleep, as the only way to protect them from potential assaults.”

item.title: Bolivia Drought El Niño 2026 - DREF Operation (MDRBO023)
item.description:
Country: Bolivia (Plurinational State of)
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Description of the Event

Date when the trigger was met

31-10-2026

What happened, where and when?

Bolivia is facing a severe, prolonged slow-onset drought affecting extensive areas of the Altiplano, the Inter-Andean Valleys, and El Chaco region simultaneously. Reduced rainfall, combined with above-average seasonal temperatures and the depletion of both surface and groundwater sources, has significantly impacted the availability of water for human consumption, agricultural production, livestock, and the livelihoods of thousands of rural households. The water shortage is also increasing community vulnerability to health risks, food insecurity, and temporary displacement in search of water and economic opportunities.

The situation is unfolding within a context of multiple climate-related risks. While the impacts of the drought persist, several regions of the country are also facing the likelihood of hazards associated with the 2026-2027 El Niño phenomenon, including frost, hailstorms, wildfires, flash floods, and flooding. These events could further exacerbate existing conditions and generate additional humanitarian impacts. The scale of the crisis exceeds the regular response capacities of several municipal and departmental autonomous governments, requiring the mobilization of extraordinary resources and enhanced inter-institutional coordination at the national level. Given the magnitude of the situation, the National Council for Risk Reduction and Disaster and/or Emergency Response (CONARADE) reviewed the evolution of the crisis and recommended the declaration of a national emergency through Resolution No. 014/2026, dated 30 October 2026. Consequently, the Government enacted Supreme Decree No. 5759 on 31 October 2026, activating extraordinary mechanisms for response, coordination, and resource mobilization to support emergency operations and early recovery efforts.

Throughout 2026, a progressive deterioration of water availability was observed across different regions of the country. As the dry season advanced, the impacts on water sources, crops, and livestock intensified, leading to a sustained increase in humanitarian needs.

  • Bolivian Altiplano (La Paz and Oruro Departments): Water availability for human consumption and livestock is under increasing pressure due to persistent hydrological deficits. In November 2026, water levels in Lake Titicaca at the Huatajata monitoring station were reported 0.87 m below the historical average, while key reservoirs supplying the La Paz metropolitan area were operating at relatively low storage levels, including 27.96% at Ajuankhota, 36.56% at Milluni, and 42.73% at Chacaltaya.
  • Inter-Andean Valleys (Cochabamba and Chuquisaca Departments): Below-normal rainfall conditions predominated across much of the Valleys macroregion during October 2026. According to the National Service of Meteorology and Hydrology (SENAMHI), most monitoring stations recorded fewer rainy days than normal, affecting rainfed agricultural production and increasing pressure on community water supply systems despite localized rainfall surpluses in some areas.
  • Chaco Region (Santa Cruz, Chuquisaca and Tarija): The region remains highly vulnerable due to its dependence on rainfed agriculture and livestock production and recurrent exposure to drought conditions. While rainfall conditions were mixed during October 2026, temperatures during November were forecast to reach 36-39°C across several Chaco areas, with generally limited precipitation forecast (0-10 mm) and continued exposure to conditions conducive to vegetation stress and livelihood impacts.

Situational reports from the Bolivian Red Cross indicate that the impacts vary considerably across affected departments. Water supply restrictions, agricultural losses and risks to livestock production have been reported in Chuquisaca, while Oruro has experienced significant effects on agricultural activities and camelid husbandry. In Cochabamba, particularly in municipalities of the Cono Sur region, the drying of reservoirs, lagoons and other water sources has affected both crop and livestock production. In Santa Cruz, impacts are concentrated in the Chaco region, where crop losses and pasture degradation are undermining livestock-based livelihoods. Meanwhile, in La Paz, drought conditions are occurring alongside other climate-related hazards, including heavy rainfall, hailstorms and flooding.
This diversity of impacts reflects the heterogeneous nature of the emergency and underscores the need for context-specific response measures across the affected regions.

However, due to the nationwide nature of the identified threats and the potential for simultaneous impacts associated with the 2026-2027 El Niño phenomenon, the declaration applies to the entire national territory. As a result, departments, municipalities, and communities across different regions of the country may require assistance, preparedness, and recovery interventions depending on the evolution of climatic conditions.

The declaration applies nationwide and aims to strengthen preparedness, response, and recovery, as well as to support the activation of contingency funding mechanisms. Within this context, the Bolivian Red Cross is prioritizing communities in Chuquisaca, Cochabamba, Oruro, La Paz, and Santa Cruz, based on documented needs, gaps in assistance, and the capacity of local branches.

item.title: Argentina: Landslide - DREF Final Report (MDRAR025)
item.description:
Country: Argentina
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Please refer to the attached file.

Description of the Event

Date of event

18-01-2026

What happened, where and when?

During the early morning of 18 January 2026, a landslide occurred in the Hermitte hill, in the city of Comodoro Rivadavia, Chubut province. The displacement of the terrain affected urban sectors located on unstable slopes, mainly in the Sismográfica, Los Tilos, El Marquesado, Mazarredo and Médanos neighbourhoods.

The phenomenon occurred in a context of accumulated rainfall and pre-existing geological conditions that favored the instability of the slopes of the Hermitte hill. It manifested as sudden, progressive movements of the ground, accompanied by the appearance of cracks, subsidence, and displacement. that caused damage to homes, streets, sidewalks, service networks and other urban infrastructures.

item.title: DR Congo: Rapport de la situation épidémiologique du choléra en RD Congo (Interne OMS), semaine 45, 2026
item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

I. POINTS SAILLANTS

  • Le nombre de cas suspects de choléra notifiés à la SE45 (1 719 cas dont 31 décès, létalité de 1,8 %) est légèrement plus bas (-17,47 %) par rapport à la SE44 (2 083 cas dont 46 décès, létalité de 2,2 %).
  • Il n’y a pas de nouvelle zone affectée en cette semaine 45 en revanche, trois zones sont à nouveau active après plusieurs semaines d’accalmie (dans les provinces de l’Equateur (1), de la Lomami (1) et du Lualaba (1)).
  • Les provinces endémiques ont rapporté 89 % de cas et 81 % de décès suspects de choléra.
  • La flambée épidémique de choléra au Tanganyika est en grande partie expliquée par l’interruption de la fourniture d’électricité à Kalemie suite à la panne de la station hydro-électrique de Bendera qui a entrainé l’arrêt du fonctionnement l’usine de distribution d’eau de la REGIDESO.
  • La campagne de vaccination contre le choléra le long du corridor fluvial a bien démarré en Equateur et dans le Mai Ndombe. Au Sud Kivu, tout est prêt pour le début de la campagne de vaccination contre le choléra au Sud Kivu.
  • L’intensification des affrontements et l’extension géographique des zones de conflits au Nord Kivu et au Sud Kivu engendre des déplacements massifs de populations et perturbe la mise en œuvre des activités de riposte, justifiant en grande partie la persistance des foyers épidémiques dans ces deux provinces.

item.title: Somalia Weekly Weather Forecast - Valid From 25 Nov - 01 Dec 2026
item.description:
Country: Somalia
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

Review Summary:

  • Very dry week across the country. During 17–23 November, rain was reported at only four stations: Banderbeyla (28.3 mm in 2 rainy days), Mogadishu (9.7 mm), Qansax Dheere (1.3 mm) and Cadale (0.8 mm). Satellite estimates (IMERG, 18–24 November) indicate 8–13 mm over parts of Lower Juba and less than 1 mm over the river catchments in Ethiopia.
  • Seasonal totals are almost unchanged after the dry week. By 23 November, 37 stations, 33 of them with a Deyr normal above 15 mm, had already received their full Deyr normal, including Baidoa (405.5 mm, 176% of the Deyr normal), Galkacyo (253.5 mm, 390%) and Banderbeyla (126.7 mm, 316%), which recorded the highest weekly total. Mogadishu rose to 35% of its Deyr normal, while Borama (16%), Burao (21%) and Luuq (25%) remain far below normal.
  • River levels on both rivers are falling or easing and remain well below flood-risk levels. Belet Weyne fell from 3.76 m on 18 November to 3.00 m today, 3.50 m below its moderate flood-risk level. Bulo Burti (2.16 m), Dollow (2.32 m) and Luuq (2.34 m) are also falling, and Jowhar (3.30 m) is easing after reaching 3.50 m on 23 November.
  • Flood water in Jowhar district continues to recede. Satellite images show about 46 km² of flood water in Jowhar district down from about 55 km² last week. Radio Ergo callers (12–18 November) reported river flooding on farms in Jowhar, while many callers in Galgaduud, Bay, the Juba valley and Gedo welcomed the rains

item.title: UNICEF Nepal Humanitarian Situation Report No. 9 - 23 November 2026
item.description:
Country: Nepal
Source: UN Children's Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

Highlights

  • Almost three months after the August floods, the response has transitioned to recovery, while continued humanitarian support remains necessary, particularly for winterization, protection, water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH), health, nutrition, education and cash assistance.
  • UNICEF has continued to strengthen early detection of disease threats, with no outbreaks reported since the 26 August floods. Nearly 1,500 flood-affected children have received winter clothes and thermal blankets. Mental health and psychosocial support reached 19,500 children and caregivers; 35 child-friendly spaces provide affected children with a safe place to learn, play and heal. In addition, UNICEF-established temporary learning centres (TLCs) have provided almost 1,800 children with continued access to education.
  • Nutrition services reached more than 13,000 children and 6,000 pregnant and breastfeeding women. Humanitarian cash assistance through government systems has reached 2,021 affected households in seven municipalities.
  • Recovery and reconstruction needs are substantial. The Government-led Post-Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) estimates total recovery and reconstruction needs at US$5.05 billion, including US$2.73 billion for infrastructure and US$413 million for social sectors.
  • UNICEF continues to restore essential services and rehabilitate damaged health, WASH and education systems. Rehabilitation of around 36 km of pipelines maintained or restored water access for 42,143 people. Support to construct semi-permanent TLCs continues.
  • UNICEF has received US$14.7 million of the US$17.2 million required for the humanitarian response (85 per cent funded), while early recovery and rehabilitation remain largely unfunded (31 per cent funded).

item.title: WHO Weekly Situation Update on Ongoing Health Emergency Events in South Sudan - Week #47, Date: 16 – 22 Nov 2026
item.description:
Countries: South Sudan, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Nigeria
Source: World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

PRIORITY ACTIONS

  • Sustain BVD preparedness as the DRC outbreak reaches 11,762 cases and 5,775 deaths (CFR 49.1%), with Watsa (HautUélé) now at 12 cases; maintain PoE screening (82,150 events over 21–23 Nov) and screen air arrivals at Juba. Sustain alert investigation in Yei, Morobo, Yambio and Maridi, and test BVD-negative alerts from the greater Yei region for yellow fever.
  • Support the Ministry of Health to declare the yellow fever outbreak (9 confirmed, 6 deaths across Yei and Morobo) and secure vaccine; follow up the 12 Morobo samples at NPHL and strengthen surveillance along the Yei–Morobo corridor.
  • Complete the Round 2 polio NIDs (commenced 17 Nov; 48% preliminary coverage) and intensify surveillance in Ayod after two cVDPV2 cases; launch the Malakal measles reactive campaign and support the Pigi response (130 cases).
  • Drive cholera testing toward 100% in Fangak and test Aweil West's 39 untested cases, and ship RDT positives for culture (only 3 of 126 sent), to protect the 12 Dec end-of-outbreak declaration; maintain malaria response (44,206 cases, 46% below 2025); and assess the health impact of violence in Tonj East, Lakes, Western Bahr el Ghazal and Jonglei.

item.title: World: Water as a superconnector: UN country coordination and integration
item.description:
Country: World
Source: UN Water

Please refer to the attached files.

Water connects nearly every aspect of sustainable development – from food and energy security to health, climate resilience, biodiversity, economic development and peace. But how can the United Nations better harness these connections to strengthen coordinated action at the country level?

Water as a superconnector: UN country coordination and integration brings together two products - an Assessment and a companion Compilation exploring how water can serve as an entry point for more integrated planning, programming and implementation across the UN system.

Drawing on country experiences and consultations, the assessment finds that while water is increasingly recognized as a cross-cutting development priority, this recognition does not always translate into coordinated action and measurable results. The challenge is to move from systems thinking to systems doing.

The assessment identifies institutional, financial and operational barriers to integrated action, while highlighting the importance of national leadership, effective coordination mechanisms, partnerships and catalytic financing. The accompanying compilation presents country experiences illustrating different approaches to strengthening collaboration, recognizing that there is no one-size-fits-all model.

A separate key messages document summarizes the main findings and opportunities for strengthening country-level action, including through implementation of the UN System-wide Strategy for Water and Sanitation.

item.title: Uganda: Case Study - All Voices Matter: Strengthening Protection and Community Resilience Through Inclusive Early Warning Systems
item.description:
Country: Uganda
Sources: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, Uganda Red Cross

Please refer to the attached file.

This case study showcases how the Uganda Red Cross Society, through the PASSAGE Project, is strengthening community resilience in Musas, Uganda, through an inclusive, community-led radio early warning system. The initiative improves access to timely climate and disaster risk information while empowering women, youth and persons with disabilities to participate in community decision-making. It highlights the role of locally led early warning systems in enhancing disaster preparedness, promoting gender equality, strengthening social cohesion, and protecting vulnerable communities.

item.title: Joint press release - Government of Nepal and United Nations underscore the urgent need to end gender-based violence and address the cost of inaction [EN/NE]
item.description:
Country: Nepal
Sources: Government of Nepal, UN Country Team in Nepal

Please refer to the attached files.

2026 campaign focuses on ensuring justice, protecting survivors and ending impunity.

KATHMANDU, 25 November 2026: Marking the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women and the launch of the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence, the Ministry of Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities and Social Security and the United Nations in Nepal underscore the urgent need to ensure justice, protect survivors and end impunity.

Despite significant progress in legal and institutional protections, gender-based violence continues to undermine the rights, dignity, safety and economic independence of women and girls in Nepal.

According to the Nepal Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS) 2022, 23 per cent of women aged 15–49 have experienced physical violence since the age of 15, while 8% have experienced sexual violence. Alarmingly, 58 per cent of women who have experienced physical or sexual violence have neither sought help nor disclosed their experience to anyone.

Beyond its consequences for survivors' physical and mental health, gender-based violence carries significant social and economic costs through interrupted education, lost income and reduced workforce participation. A preliminary estimate for Nepal suggests that violence-related disruption to paid work alone could account for approximately NPR 3.6 billion in lost economic value annually.

“Every woman and girl has the right to live free from violence and fear. Nepal has made important progress in establishing legal and institutional protections. Our priority is to ensure that these commitments translate into accessible justice, effective protection and meaningful support for every survivor,” said Honourable Sita Badi, Minister of Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities and Social Security.

“Laws only matter when they work for survivors - we must ensure timely justice and real accountability,” said Honourable Kamala Parajuli, Chairperson of the National Women Commission.

This year's global UNiTE campaign, “Ensure Justice, Protect Survivors, End Impunity,” comes at a significant time for Nepal, with ongoing legislative reforms presenting an opportunity to address barriers to justice, strengthen accountability and respond to emerging forms of violence, including technology-facilitated gender-based violence.

“Accelerating the implementation of Nepal's CEDAW Roadmap, strengthening justice institutions and expanding access to legal aid and survivor-centred services are critical. We must also ensure safe workplaces, invest in the leadership of women's rights organizations and challenge the social norms that perpetuate violence. No woman should have to choose between her safety and her livelihood,” said Jaco du Toit, United Nations Resident Coordinator a.i. in Nepal.

To mark the campaign's launch, the Ministry, together with the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and with support from the United Nations in Nepal, convened a High-Level National Dialogue on “The Cost of Inaction: Access to Justice and Accountability for Ending Gender-Based Violence in Nepal” in Kathmandu today.

A multi-sectoral panel discussion brought together perspectives from government, justice institutions, civil society, survivor advocates, the private sector and the media to examine the cost of delayed and inaccessible justice and identify practical measures to address existing gaps.

The Ministry and the United Nations in Nepal reaffirm their commitment to sustaining collective action beyond the 16 Days of Activism, with concrete commitments, stronger partnerships and measurable progress towards ending violence against women and girls.
item.author: Government of Nepal
UN Country Team in Nepal

item.title: DR Congo: Crise Humanitaire Complexe et Épidémies - République démocratique du Congo : Rapport de Situation Semaine No 45 (2 au 8 novembre 2026)
item.description:
Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo
Source: World Health Organization

Please refer to the attached file.

Résumé de la situation épidémiologique et humanitaire

Situation épidémiologique

  • Épidémie de MVE : Depuis le début de l’épidémie jusqu’au 8 novembre 2026 (S45), 10 990 cas confirmés et 5 354 décès (létalité : 48,7 %) ont été rapportés dans 67/178 (37,6 %) ZS de 8 provinces, avec 2 951 guéris et 966 patients en isolement/CTE. L’Ituri demeure l’épicentre (69,6 % ; 7 654 cas), suivie du Nord-Kivu (24,7 % ; 2 720 cas). Sur la S45 (2–8 novembre), 458 nouveaux cas et 228 décès ont été notifiés, dont 70 cas (Ituri 40, Nord-Kivu 23, Haut-Uélé 5, Tshopo 2) et 31 décès confirmés (22 communautaires et 9 intra-CTE) le 8 novembre. L’Initiative « Fleuve Congo sans Ebola » cible 4 hubs fluviaux : Kisangani, Mbandaka, Kwamouth et Kinshasa/Maluku.
  • Épidémie de choléra : Un total de 66 116 cas suspects et 1 909 décès (létalité : 2,9 %) a été rapporté de la S01 à la S45/2026 dans 250/519 (48,2 %) ZS de 21 DPS, contre 63 243 cas et 1 906 décès (3,0 %) à la même période en 2025 (+4,5 %). À la S45/2026, une baisse hebdomadaire de 17,5 % est observée avec 1 719 cas suspects et 31 décès (létalité : 1,8 %) dans 66 ZS de 14 DPS (contre 2 083 cas et 46 décès à la S44), dominés par le Sud-Kivu (564 cas), le Nord-Kivu (479 cas) et le Haut-Katanga (302 cas). Au total, 26 ZS sont en épidémie active.
  • Épidémie de mpox : Après exclusion de l’erreur d’encodage d’Opala (Tshopo, 413 cas erronés), 194 cas suspects et 2 décès (létalité : 1,0 %) ont été notifiés à la S45/2026 dans 31 ZS de 13 DPS, contre 287 cas et 1 décès (0,3 %) à la S44 (-32,4 %). De la S01 à la S45/2026, 34 585 cas suspects et 393 décès (1,1 %) ont été rapportés dans 372 ZS de 26 DPS (contre 84 715 cas et 797 décès en 2025, soit -59,2 %). À Kinshasa, la rétro-saisie à la Clinique Kinoise a consolidé 1 192 enregistrements uniques.
  • Épidémie de rougeole : À la S45/2026, 229 cas suspects et 4 décès (létalité : 1,7 %) ont été notifiés en SIMR dans 45 ZS de 12 DPS (chiffres identiques au bulletin spécifique rougeole du 17/11). De S01 à S45/2026, 130 697 cas et 1 680 décès (1,3 %) ont été notifiés dans 496/519 (95,6 %) ZS de 26 DPS (+54,1 % vs 2025 ; 162 ZS en épidémie). Le Bloc 1 de la campagne RR (19 provinces) a vacciné 34 221 981 enfants (CV adm. 103,8 % ; MI 82,9 %) et le Bloc 2 (7 provinces) débutera le 27/11/2026.
  • Situation humanitaire (Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Ituri) : Au moins 92 incidents sécuritaires ont été rapportés à la S45 (55 au Sud-Kivu, 20 au Nord-Kivu, ≥17 en Ituri) : combats à Fataki (Ituri) suspendant depuis le 07/11 les mouvements sur Gina–Fataki et Fataki–Bule (76 000 PDI affectés à Plaine Savo), saisie de 2 camions PAM à Shabunda (Sud-Kivu), afflux de 7 561 déplacés à Kibarizo (ZS Mweso, Nord-Kivu) avec flambée de choléra (11 cas), diarrhées graves (280 cas) et malnutrition (+55 %), et prise en charge de 148 nouveaux blessés balistiques (138 au Sud-Kivu, 10 en Ituri ; cumul de 6 053 blessés) et 75 VVS au Sud-Kivu.

item.title: Brazil: ACNUR agradece la contribución de Japón para apoyar a las personas refugiadas y desplazadas por la fuerza en Brasil y Ecuador
item.description:
Countries: Brazil, Ecuador, Japan
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

CIUDAD DE PANAMÁ – ACNUR, la Agencia de la ONU para los Refugiados, acoge con satisfacción la generosa contribución de 2 millones de dólares estadounidenses (USD) del Gobierno de Japón para apoyar el proyecto “Fortalecimiento de la Protección y Promoción de la Inclusión Socioeconómica de las Personas Desplazadas”, un proyecto regional que fortalecerá la protección, ampliará el acceso a derechos y servicios, y promoverá la inclusión socioeconómica de las personas refugiadas y desplazadas por la fuerza en Brasil y Ecuador.

La financiación apoyará actividades durante un período de 12 meses, con las que se prevé beneficiar a aproximadamente 19.500 personas refugiadas y otras personas con necesidades de protección internacional, así como a miembros de las comunidades de acogida, mediante iniciativas diseñadas para fortalecer los sistemas de protección, ampliar las oportunidades económicas y reforzar la capacidad de las autoridades locales y las comunidades que responden al desplazamiento.

“ACNUR agradece profundamente al Gobierno y al pueblo de Japón por su constante solidaridad y apoyo”, afirmó Isabel Márquez, Directora Regional de ACNUR para las Américas. “En un momento en que muchas personas refugiadas y desplazadas por la fuerza siguen enfrentando riesgos de protección y obstáculos para su inclusión, la contribución de Japón ayudará a generar mayores oportunidades de seguridad, autosuficiencia y dignidad, al tiempo que fortalecerá a las comunidades que las acogen”.

El proyecto se articula en torno a tres pilares complementarios: el fortalecimiento de los sistemas de asilo y del acceso a la protección; la promoción de la estabilización y la inclusión socioeconómica; y el refuerzo de la capacidad de municipios y comunidades que se encuentran en la primera línea de recepción y apoyo a las poblaciones desplazadas.

En Brasil, el proyecto apoyará la mejora del acceso a la protección y la documentación, ampliará las oportunidades de medios de vida y empleabilidad, y fortalecerá los servicios municipales y los mecanismos comunitarios de protección en las zonas que acogen a importantes poblaciones refugiadas. La iniciativa también respaldará los esfuerzos para facilitar el acceso a oportunidades económicas sostenibles y promover la integración local.

En Ecuador, el proyecto fortalecerá el acceso a los servicios de asilo y protección, mejorará la gestión de casos y las derivaciones hacia servicios esenciales, promoverá el emprendimiento y la inclusión económica, y apoyará a los gobiernos locales y organizaciones comunitarias que desempeñan un papel fundamental en el fortalecimiento de la cohesión social y la resiliencia.

La iniciativa refleja el compromiso sostenido Japón con la promoción de la seguridad humana y el apoyo a soluciones duraderas para las poblaciones desplazadas por la fuerza. A través de contribuciones específicas en sistemas de protección, medios de vida y capacidades locales, el proyecto contribuirá a que las personas refugiadas y desplazadas por la fuerza reconstruyan sus vidas y aporten de manera positiva a las comunidades que las acogen.

En toda la región de las Américas, el desplazamiento continúa siendo impulsado por la violencia, la inseguridad, las violaciones de los derechos humanos, las presiones económicas y los impactos relacionados con el clima. La mayoría de las personas refugiadas y desplazadas por la fuerza permanecen dentro de la región, buscando seguridad y oportunidades en países vecinos. Fortalecer los sistemas nacionales de protección sigue siendo fundamental para garantizar la protección, fomentar la autosuficiencia y promover la convivencia pacífica en las comunidades afectadas por el desplazamiento.

  • Melanie Gallant, gallant@unhcr.org

item.title: Afghanistan: Impact of the Bans and Restrictions on Women Working for NGOs, INGOs and the UN - Round 16 (October 2026)
item.description:
Country: Afghanistan
Sources: Asia Pacific Gender in Humanitarian Action Working Group, UN Women

Please refer to the attached Infographic.

This snapshot presents findings from the sixteenth round of the GCG and HAWG survey on the impact of the bans and other gender-related restrictions on Afghan women working for NGOs, INGOs and the UN. Responses were collected from 7 to 26 October 2026 from 90 organizations: 72 NNGOs and CSOs (62 of them WLOs), 10 INGOs and 8 UN agencies. This round has more respondents working on GBV (60%, from 44% in June) and on human rights and gender equality (69%, from 59%).

Restrictions on women's participation in humanitarian and BHN operations remain widespread, despite a decline in reports of new formal instructions. While 36% of organizations reported no new instructions or impediments, practical barriers persist: half report that women staff cannot report to the office in some provinces, and 32% report women staff stopped by the PVPV on the way to work, the highest level across all rounds. Only 42% remain fully operating with women and men, and fewer hold agreements with the DfA for women to work at project locations and offices. With 66% accepting DfA conditions to keep operating, the findings suggest a shift from new formal restrictions towards more persistent enforcement.

item.title: Uganda National Baseline Survey on School Feeding (December 2025)
item.description:
Country: Uganda
Source: Government of Uganda

Please refer to the attached file.

Uganda’s National Baseline Survey on School Feeding provides a comprehensive national picture of the coverage, quality and delivery of school meals in primary schools. Led by the Ministry of Education and Sports, the survey establishes an important evidence base to inform policy, programming, investment and future monitoring of school feeding across the country.

The findings show that 46 percent of primary school learners receive school meals, with significant disparities across regions and school types. Coverage is highest in Karamoja, Kampala and Buganda North, and lowest in Tooro, Ankole and West Nile, while rural, public and day schools generally have lower coverage. Critically, around 30 percent of learners do not eat any meal while at school, highlighting the continued challenge of hunger during the school day. The report also identifies gaps in dietary diversity, financing, procurement, infrastructure and management, and recommends expanding coverage in underserved areas, improving the nutritional quality of meals, strengthening local procurement and financing, and integrating school feeding more systematically into national education planning and monitoring.

item.title: Brazil: PAHO calls for stronger surveillance amid increase in mpox cases in the Americas
item.description:
Countries: Brazil, World
Source: Pan American Health Organization

Washington, D.C., 25 November 2026 (PAHO) – The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) is urging countries in the Americas to strengthen surveillance, laboratory capacity and prevention measures, including vaccination, in response to a surge in mpox cases in several countries of the Region.

In an Epidemiological Alert issued on 24 November, PAHO highlights an increase in cases since epidemiological week 39 of 2026, primarily in Brazil, alongside the growing detection of mpox clade Ib in the Region.

From January to November 2026, 13 countries reported 3,269 confirmed cases and four deaths. Since 2022, 76,084 cases and 202 deaths have been reported across 31 countries and territories in the Americas. Brazil has reported 1,325 cases in 2026, including one death, with an increase since September.

Mpox continues to disproportionately affect men who have sex with men. Of the 114 reported mpox deaths for which HIV status was known, 111 (97%) were among people with HIV.

PAHO is urging health authorities to strengthen epidemiological and genomic surveillance to ensure timely detection and investigation of cases, monitor changes in transmission patterns, and reinforce targeted prevention and control measures, including vaccination, particularly among populations at increased risk.

What is mpox and how can it be prevented?

Mpox is an infectious disease caused by the mpox virus. It can spread through close physical contact with someone who has the infection, including skin-to-skin and intimate contact, as well as through contact with contaminated materials such as clothing and bedding.

Symptoms commonly include a skin rash or lesions, fever, headache, muscle aches, back pain, fatigue and swollen lymph nodes. The rash can appear on the face, hands, feet, genital and anal areas, and inside the mouth or throat.

Anyone who develops an unexplained rash or other symptoms consistent with mpox should seek medical advice and testing, particularly if they have had close contact with someone who may have the infection.

Vaccination is recommended for groups at high risk of infection, based on each country's epidemiological situation. Travelers belonging to higher-risk groups are advised to seek vaccination before traveling to areas with active transmission. Vaccination should complement, not replace, other prevention measures.

Background

On 14 August 2024, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared mpox a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC) following the international spread of cases and the risk of sustained transmission. The emergency designation was lifted on 5 September 2025, after the global impact of the outbreak had decreased and surveillance and response capacities had strengthened.

The end of the PHEIC did not mean that mpox had ceased to pose a public health risk. The virus continues to circulate, with different clades detected in several regions and new transmission patterns emerging. PAHO's latest alert underscores the importance of maintaining surveillance and preparedness to detect and respond to cases promptly.

item.title: From Rainfall Forecasts to Anticipatory Action: A Flood Digital Twin at Work in Dolo Ado, Ethiopia (November 2026)
item.description:
Country: Ethiopia
Source: CGIAR

Please refer to the attached file.

Citation

Haile, Alemseged Tamiru, Eden Seifu Gebre, Getahun Kebede Mengistie, Abel Negussie Alemu, and Hugox Retief. 2026. From Rainfall Forecasts to Anticipatory Action: A Flood Digital Twin at Work in Dolo Ado, Ethiopia. International Water Management Institute.

Abstract/Description

Flood Early Warning Bulletins translate forecasts into clear, timely, actionable information for preparedness, anticipatory action, and emergency response. By presenting expected conditions, potential impacts, and recommended actions in a standard format, they help government agencies, humanitarian organizations, and at-risk communities coordinate decisions before floods occur. Yet fragmented datasets, disconnected modelling workflows, and manual processes often delay bulletins and shorten the time available to protect lives, livelihoods, and infrastructure.

To address this gap, the International Water Management Institute (IWMI), national government institutions, and development partners developed the Dolo Ado Digital Twin-based Flood Early Warning System. It creates a digital replica of the floodplain, enables two-way data exchange with communities, and integrates global databases, field surveys, and district data. HEC-HMS converts rainfall forecasts into flood forecasts, while HEC-RAS simulates likely inundation, including water depth and flood duration across the river and floodplain.

A key achievement is the co-created Flood Early Warning Bulletin, refined by stakeholders through consultations, co-design workshops, technical training, and continuous feedback. An automated workflow rapidly converts reliable Digital Twin forecasts into standardized warnings, with content, visuals, terminology, and format tailored to operational needs. The bulletin enables government agencies, humanitarian organizations, and disaster risk management authorities to make timely, coordinated decisions before and during floods.
